scope: Batches 16–19, 31 held meanings and 93 offline question bands

items.meaning: some; plural article before an adjective
items.reviewNote: In chapter IV 86:303, de means some; plural article before an adjective. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. The plural indefinite article de before an adjective differs from the published genitive preposition; both source examples match.

In chapter IV 100:68, de means some; an unspecified amount of. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. Three partitive constructions quantify confusion, variety and difficulty; they are not possession or origin.

In chapter IV 105:66, de means toward; near. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. The stones approach the eyes; this directional preposition differs from the genitive examples.

items.meaning: some; plural article before a vowel
items.reviewNote: In chapter IV 105:143, d’ means some; plural article before a vowel. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. The elided form introduces plural microscopes before an initial vowel, distinct from a genitive.

In chapter IV 108:46, d’ means of; with a described quality. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. Quelque chose d’imperceptible is an adjective-link construction, not ownership.

items.meaning: any; of after a negative quantity
items.reviewNote: In chapter IV 112:63, d’ means any; of after a negative quantity. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. Point d’esprit is negative quantity, and the elision before esprit is essential.

In chapter IV 112:154, d’ means as; in a degree comparison. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. D’aussi gros marks a degree comparison in the pronoun-adjective construction.

items.meaning: there is; there are in il y a
items.reviewNote: In chapter IV 97:46, a means there is; there are in il y a. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. Four il y a or il n’y a source uses express existence and link the published existential avoir sense with new surface questions.

In chapter IV 87:0, comme means since; because. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. Two occurrences introduce causal subordinate clauses; the published questions teach comparison.

In chapter IV 96:49, comme means how; to what degree. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. The two parallel clauses exclaim about the planet’s shape and orbit.

In chapter IV 115:28, comme means how; in the way that. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. Comme la chose se passa refers to the manner in which it occurred, not a resemblance between two things.

In chapter IV 83:92, gens means attendants; members of an entourage. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. The Sirian’s gens prepare food and travel in his entourage; the other two chapter IV gens are ordinary people.

items.meaning: where; from where in a relative clause
items.reviewNote: In chapter IV 84:48, où means where; from where in a relative clause. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. All three places are linked by relative où or d’où, whereas the published question prompts are interrogatives.

In chapter IV 90:129, non means or not; negative alternative. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. Ou non completes an alternative without a standalone no reply; non plus is a separate expression.

items.meaning: to refer to; mean by speaking
items.reviewNote: In chapter IV 95:412, parler means to refer to; mean by speaking. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. The parenthetical narrator clarifies that grains refers to mountains, rather than the act of speech.

items.meaning: were; formed a passive with cut
items.reviewNote: In chapter IV 105:118, étaient means were; formed a passive with cut. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. The diamonds were cut or faceted; the source uses passive être, not the published linking examples.

In chapter IV 113:111, été means been; gone to do something. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. Avaient été faire observations describes their earlier journey to perform research, not a static property.

In chapter IV 105:39, aperçut means realized; noticed a fact. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. S’aperçut que reports a realization, matching the published notice sense rather than the exact surface’s glimpse questions.

In chapter IV 94:126, certaines means some; certain unspecified stars. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. Certaines means some stars, linked to the published unspecified determiner sense, not sure/certain.

items.meaning: finger; a digit on the hand
items.reviewNote: In chapter IV 109:25, doigt means finger; a digit on the hand. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. The little finger holds the whale literally; published questions center on figurative toucher du doigt.

In chapter IV 95:325, grains means small pointed projections. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. The narrator’s parenthesis identifies the pointed grains as mountains at the giant’s scale.

In chapter IV 110:54, imagina means supposed; assumed. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. S’imagina means supposed the whale-only population, separate from devising a device.

In chapter IV 104:114, livres means pounds; weight units. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. The number measures diamond weight; all middle-band alternatives are feminine plural nouns of different semantic categories.

In chapter IV 87:270, marche means walks; moves on foot. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. The finite verb means walks on feet and links the published marcher walking sense, not the same-spelled marche noun.

In chapter IV 111:123, moyen means possibility; way to believe. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. Pas moyen de croire denies possibility, rather than naming a concrete method.

In chapter IV 84:43, pays means region; tract of land. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. The tiny land they inspect is a local region, not necessarily a politically bounded country.

In chapter IV 87:123, plutôt means or rather; more precisely. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. Ou plutôt replaces the preceding claim about the Sun with the Earth; published questions emphasize preference.

In chapter IV 84:22, reconnaître means to survey; explore. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. The travelers survey unfamiliar terrain; they do not acknowledge guilt or recognize a known person.

In chapter IV 114:105, sauver means escape; get to safety. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. Se sauver after the grounding means escape the peril oneself, not rescue another person.

items.meaning: aid; means provided by an instrument
items.reviewNote: In chapter IV 107:62, secours means aid; means provided by an instrument. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. Par leur secours makes the microscopes the means, distinct from aid to an injured person.

In chapter IV 113:38, volée means flock; group of people. The published exact-form question set teaches another construction or meaning; these three offline bands review the source context. A volée of philosophers is a group, not the existing same-spelled stolen participle.
